items.title: Ghana’s industrial dream at risk? How the Yuan policy could deepen China dependence
items.description: Bank of Ghana’s new payment rule will ease the demand for dollars. A look at the trade data shows why it could also deepen a dependence Ghana can least afford. Ghana’s importers no longer have to hunt for US dollars to buy Chinese goods. Under a new Bank of Ghana policy, businesses can pay for goods from China directly in Chinese Yuan (RMB), and they can receive payments in Yuan too. For any Ghanaian who has seen how a high dollar rate makes imports expensive, this looks like good news. But the trade data tells a more complicated story, and it starts with one uncomfortable fact: Ghana already buys far more from China than it can pay for with what it sells. Over the past eight years, China has consistently been Ghana’s largest source of imports. The most recent data, for 2024, shows that Ghana’s import bill from China alone stood at $9.84 billion. This was equivalent to 61.5 percent of Ghana’s total exports to all countries that year, which stood at $16 billion. This tells you that Ghana already depends heavily on China for its imports. The picture gets sharper when you look at total imports. Ghana bought $20.4 billion worth of goods from the world in 2024. Chinese goods made up 48.2% of that, so almost one in every two dollars Ghana spends abroad goes to a single country. Money does not flow back at the same pace. In 2024, Ghana sold only about $2 billion worth of goods to China. That means Ghana bought nearly five dollars’ worth of Chinese products for every dollar it sold there. A gap this wide is not new. What is new is a policy that makes buying even easier. The change works because of a Chinese payment network called the Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS). It launched on October 8, 2015, to clear and settle yuan payments across borders, and it has been built up steadily since. Behind the network is a larger goal. Beijing wants the yuan to be used more widely around the world, and the system is a key tool for that. By 2015, the yuan had already become China’s second-largest cross-border payment currency and the fourth-largest payment currency globally. For Ghana, joining this system means payments to China become faster and simpler. It also means Ghana’s trade is wired more closely into China’s financial infrastructure. The upside is clear. If importers pay in Yuan, they need fewer dollars. That takes pressure off the dollar market, where supply has often fallen short of demand. The risk is in what cheaper, easier payments encourage. When buying from China gets simpler, the incentive to buy rather than to produce gets stronger. Local manufacturers already compete against Chinese products that arrive in large volumes and often at low prices. Easier payment can widen that advantage. Over time, Ghana risks becoming a market for other countries’ goods rather than a maker of its own, which would weaken local businesses and the country’s wider capacity to produce. The policy solves a payment problem. It does not solve a production problem, and the data shows the production problem is the bigger one. If Ghana pairs the Yuan rule with real support for local manufacturers, such as cheaper financing, reliable power and a stronger push for exports, the dollar relief could give the economy room to grow. Without that, the likely result is simple: more imports, a wider trade gap, and a deeper dependence on one trading partner.

items.title: ‘The world thanks you’ — Neymar bids farewell to Messi ahead of Argentina final game
items.description: By Adegboyega Adeleye Brazilian football star Neymar has paid an emotional tribute to Lionel Messi ahead of the Argentine captain’s final appearance for the country against Benin at the Estadio Monumental in Buenos Aires on Wednesday. Messi is set to make his final appearance for Argentina against Benin, with tributes pouring in for the 39-year-old after an illustrious international career with the Albiceleste. Neymar, who shared the pitch with Messi at Barcelona from 2013 to 2017 and Paris Saint-Germain from 2021 to 2023, joined the tributes with a heartfelt message on his official Instagram account. “Everyone who loves football has enjoyed your talent over the years. Today will be your last match in the shirt of your national team, your country, and I hope you enjoy every moment, and that all the words of appreciation offered to you today bring you joy,” Neymar wrote. “It is not Argentina alone that thanks you, but the entire world thanks you for everything you have given to football,” he added. “Thank you for making me love football even more. It was an honour for me to play against you, and most importantly, to make history with you. Thank you, Lionel Messi.” View this post on Instagram Messi has enjoyed a remarkable career with Argentina, winning three major international titles — the Copa America in 2021 and 2024, and the 2022 FIFA World Cup. His final appearance for the national team will bring an end to an international career that has seen him establish himself as one of Argentina’s most decorated players. items.title: NSITF exposes fake recruitment scam, cautions Nigerians against fraudsters
items.description: By Johnbosco Agbakwuru ABUJA – The Nigeria Social Insurance Trust Fund (NSITF) has issued a public warning over the spread of fraudulent employment advertisements and forged appointment letters being used by scammers to deceive job seekers. The warning was contained in a public notice issued by the Fund and circulated to regional and branch managers via a memorandum dated October 5, 2026, signed by Samaila Abdu, Esq., Executive Director, Administration. According to the notice, the NSITF said it is not currently recruiting for any position and described employment advertisements circulating on social media, particularly Facebook, as fake The Fund stated that the fraudulent advertisements reflect a growing trend of individuals and groups falsely claiming to represent the NSITF in recruitment exercises. NSITF urged members of the public to disregard such advertisements and avoid making payments to anyone over purported employment opportunities. The Fund emphasised that it neither charges fees for employment nor conducts recruitment through unofficial social media platforms or channels. It added that any genuine employment opportunities would be announced through its official channels. “Stay alert, stay safe,” the Fund urged, advising members of the public who encounter suspicious recruitment advertisements or requests to avoid responding and report them to the appropriate NSITF authorities. As part of measures to protect the public and safeguard the integrity of its recruitment process, NSITF management has directed all Regional and Branch Managers to prominently display the public notice at strategic locations within their offices. The directive covers reception areas, main entrances and exits, notice boards, SERVICOM desks and other conspicuous locations accessible to staff and members of the public. The Fund said the notice should be displayed immediately and kept visible to ensure that members of the public are adequately informed and protected from fraudulent recruitment activities. NSITF urged Nigerians, particularly job seekers, to exercise caution and verify every recruitment claim through the Fund’s official communication channels before taking any action. The development comes amid growing concerns over fraudulent online recruitment schemes targeting unemployed Nigerians with promises of government jobs in exchange for money or personal information. NSITF’s latest warning underscores the need for job seekers to remain vigilant, as legitimate public-sector recruitment does not require applicants to pay individuals or unofficial agents for employment. items.title: Teachers’ strike: Government has funds, but processes are causing delays – Education Committee Vice Chair
items.description: The Vice Chairman of Parliament’s Education Committee, Joseph Kumah, says government has funds to meet its financial obligations to teachers, but administrative processes are contributing to delays in settling some of the outstanding payments. Speaking on Joy FM’s Top Story on Tuesday, October 6, Mr Kumah said the Education Committee has been monitoring the dispute between government and the pre-tertiary teacher unions and has engaged stakeholders in an effort to help resolve the impasse. According to him, the concerns raised by the unions, including the 20% deprived-area allowance and promotion arrears, largely involve administrative processes such as uploading and validating data. “Our findings, our checks, are that it is not about financial constraint. There’s money available to pay, but it’s the processes.” He said the collective bargaining agreement is also a major issue under discussion, with negotiations covering matters such as management allowance, continuous professional development allowance and digital allowance. Mr Kumah said Parliament’s Education Committee recognises the concerns of the teachers and believes they deserve to receive commitments made to them. “Anybody that is promised something definitely, they should receive that promise.” However, he appealed to the striking teachers to consider the impact of their continued absence from the classroom on pupils, particularly as the industrial action affects teaching and learning across the country. He said the committee would continue to monitor the situation and engage the relevant institutions, while respecting the roles of the Ministry of Education and other agencies responsible for managing the negotiations. Mr Kumah also noted that Education Minister Haruna Iddrisu had given an assurance that all outstanding promotion arrears would be paid by October 30. He said Parliament would continue to monitor the government’s commitments and intervene where necessary to ensure the concerns of both parties are addressed. His comments follow renewed negotiations between the teacher unions, the Fair Wages and Salaries Commission and the Ghana Education Service, as efforts continue to resolve the nationwide strike by pre-tertiary teachers.

Dar warns of 'serious implications' for regional peace, security if Pakistan deprived of water share under IWT
items.description: Attempts to deprive Pakistan of its rightful share of water would have “serious implications” for regional peace and security, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said on Tuesday, in an address regarding the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT). The deputy premier was addressing the International Water Symposium convened by the Embassy of Pakistan in Austria in collaboration with the Diplomatic Academy of Vienna, according to the Foreign Office. Water and the IWT remain a contentious issue between India and Pakistan, following New Delhi’s unilateral abeyance of the accord in April last year after an attack on tourists in India-occupied Kashmir. The development preceded a brief military conflict between the two sides in May 2025. In his keynote address delivered via video message, Dar stressed that there should be “no misunderstanding” about Pakistan’s resolve to safeguard its rights and interests under the IWT and international law. “Any attempt to deprive Pakistan of the waters rightfully allocated to it would have serious implications for regional peace and security,” he said. Stressing that water was fundamental to human survival, prosperity and environmental sustainability, Dar pointed out that its availability was increasingly determining the stability of relations among states. He added that for countries sharing transboundary river systems, a “permanent interdependence” was created by their geography. “The fundamental question, therefore, is whether shared waters will be governed through cooperation and agreed legal frameworks, or become instruments of political pressure and confrontation,” he said. For Pakistan in particular, the deputy premier added, water security was inseparable from food security, as the waters of the Indus River System sustained the lives and livelihoods of over 250 million people in the country. He highlighted that this water sustained agriculture, food security, energy production, economic development, and life-supporting ecological systems. “Any attempt to undermine Pakistan’s rights over these waters carries consequences that extend far beyond a bilateral disagreement,” DPM Dar stressed. The IWT, which Pakistan signed in 1960 after a decade of negotiation, replaced what the deputy premier termed “upstream discretion” with binding legal obligations, establishing a framework of “certainty and predictability” for both countries. This, he said, reflected a fundamental recognition that “waters upon which millions depend must remain insulated from the fluctuations in political relations”. However, he said, this principle was now being challenged as India had unilaterally placed the treaty “in abeyance” in April 2025, although it contained no provision permitting either party to do so. He highlighted that on Aug 31, the Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) had issued a unanimous award on the status of the IWT, ordering India to uphold the treaty and restricting its work on a hydropower project. The PCA had unequivocally confirmed that the treaty “remains fully in force” and that India remained bound by its obligations under it, as there were no grounds justifying its suspension or termination. “This is an important reaffirmation of Pakistan’s position, as well as a fundamental principle of international law,” Dar stated. “ Pacta sunt servanda: agreements must be kept.” The deputy premier stressed that the court’s decision reinforced that the rights and obligations established under the IWT could not be displaced unilaterally. However, he pointed out that India continued its “intransigent behaviour and illegal actions”. “Pakistan has consistently sought to address its differences with India through dialogue, diplomacy and the dispute resolution mechanisms provided under the treaty,” he said, adding that the country was also participating in the Neutral Expert proceedings under the treaty administered by the PCA’s Vienna Office. He emphasised Pakistan’s constructive participation in both the Neutral Expert proceedings and the PCA’s award processes, which he said demonstrated the country’s confidence in the IWT’s institutional mechanisms. The deputy premier highlighted that the credibility of international law depended “not only on the conclusion of treaties, but also upon their faithful implementation and respect for decisions rendered under their agreed procedures” — a principle Pakistan had consistently upheld, he added. Dar stressed the “profound” humanitarian, economic and security implications of the use of water as an “instrument of pressure”. He added that India’s illegal actions had implications extending beyond the region, as they would establish a “dangerous precedent” for other transboundary river basins that relied on international agreements. “Amidst challenges to the international law-based world order, the international community should be strengthening treaty-based cooperation, not permitting its erosion,” he said. “The principles of equitable and reasonable utilisation, the prevention of significant transboundary harm, and cooperation remain essential to international water governance. Their application must, however, respect the specific rights and obligations established under the treaties governing individual river systems.” The deputy premier also highlighted Pakistan’s continued commitment to dialogue, diplomacy and the peaceful settlement of disputes and termed cooperation over shared waters “indispensable” to regional peace, development and sustainability. He said that the way forward depended on three fundamental principles: the implementation of the IWT in letter and spirit; for all differences and disputes to be addressed through its established mechanisms and for these decisions to be respected; and the strengthening of technical engagement, transparency and data-sharing by both countries in accordance with the treaty. “Our preference remains clear: cooperation over coercion, dialogue over confrontation, and the rule of law over unilateralism,” DPM Dar said. “The future of transboundary water governance must rest on cooperation, mutual respect, and the faithful implementation of international obligations. Pakistan stands ready to pursue this path.” The IWT allocates the eastern rivers — Ravi, Beas and Sutlej — to India, while the western rivers — Indus, Jhelum and Chenab — are largely allocated to Pakistan. The 1960 water-sharing agreement has also established mechanisms for data-sharing and dispute resolution. In April 2025, India announced a unilateral suspension of its obligations under the treaty, following an attack on tourists in India-occupied Kashmir’s Pahalgam that killed 26 — an incident New Delhi blamed on Islamabad without evidence, while Islamabad denied the allegations. Following India’s actions, Pakistan termed any attempt to suspend its water share an “act of war”, noting the IWT had no provision for unilateral suspension. It later argued that Delhi’s action was a violation of the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties. In its order, the PCA backed Pakistan’s stance, declaring that the IWT between the two countries remained fully in force, as India had no justification for ending or suspending the agreement. However, in a statement issued by its foreign ministry, India — which is officially a member of the intergovernmental court — said it did not recognise the court and “categorically” rejected the verdict.

items.title: Ronaldo rules out Portugal return while Jesus remains coach — report
items.description: By Adegboyega Adeleye Cristiano Ronaldo has reportedly decided against returning to the Portugal national team while Jorge Jesus remains head coach, following a dispute over an expected public apology, sources have told ESPN. According to ESPN, Ronaldo is upset that Jesus did not offer the previously agreed apology during his most recent news conference. Recall Jesus had said after Portugal’s 2-1 Nations League win over Norway on Sunday that the door remained open for Ronaldo to return. “If he wants to, he’ll return to the national team,” Jesus said. “We can talk before the next call-up, but Cris is the one who’s going to decide. “In my first call-up, I said, ‘I need you, I need you to be close to me, playing or not playing, I need you.’ And now I’m saying the same thing.” However, sources told ESPN that because Jesus stopped short of specifically apologising, Ronaldo has now opted not to return to the national team for as long as Jesus remains in charge. Ronaldo left the Portugal squad after he was an unused substitute in the 2-1 Nations League victory away to Norway on September 27. The Al Nassr forward subsequently vowed to “tell the truth” about the dispute, which has cast further uncertainty over his international future and resumed to training with his club in Saudi Arabia on Monday. Ronaldo, who has scored a record 146 goals in 234 appearances for Portugal, has not made any further public comment on the matter. ESPN also said it contacted the Portugal Football Federation for comment. The post Ronaldo rules out Portugal return while Jesus remains coach — report appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: UN chief hails Pakistan's 'pivotal role' in US-Iran conflict, calls for 'return to diplomacy'
items.description: United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres on Tuesday lauded Pakistan’s “pivotal role” in mediating between the United States and Iran as he called on the parties to end the conflict and return to diplomacy. Addressing a press conference in Islamabad alongside Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, he said: “Pakistan’s spirit of engagement is front and centre on issues of international peace and security. “I salute Pakistan’s leadership for helping to create the conditions for dialogue between the US and Iran and mediating that conflict. Your efforts helped deliver the Islamabad memorandum of understanding , the subsequent ceasefire and the framework for future negotiations . Every Pakistani should be proud of that pivotal role,” he said. “And from Islamabad, I want to send a loud and clear message to all parties: end the conflict, return to diplomacy and restore navigational rights in accordance with international law. There will never be peace in the region until the right of self-determination of the Palestinian people is recognised, as Pakistan has long championed,” he said. At the outset of his speech, the UN chief said that it was “wonderful to be back in Pakistan”. “I am in the closing months of my tenure as UN secretary general. Before that, I served ten years as UN high commissioner for refugees,” he said. “Pakistan has shown that, even in difficult circumstances, perhaps especially in difficult circumstances, compassion and responsibility must go hand-in-hand,” he said. He asserted that Pakistan mattered not only because of its size, but because it brought an “essential perspective” to global debates. “For decades, Pakistan opened its doors to millions of Afghans fleeing conflict and instability. Communities around this country shared whatever they had with people seeking protection and safety,” Guterres said. He added that the UN was committed to working together with the country to uphold protection principles and ensure that returns of Afghans “proceed in a voluntary, safe and dignified way”. According to the UN chief, Pakistan had put a spotlight on the value of multilateralism, dialogue, mediation and diplomacy at a time of growing division and mistrust around the world. “Those same values are vital within societies as well,” he stated. “Here and around the world, we know that inclusive institutions, respect for human rights, and a vibrant civic space are necessary to help strengthen social cohesion, build trust and enable people to contribute fully to their country’s future.” Guterres also appreciated Pakistan’s contributions to United Nations peacekeeping. “Pakistani women and men have served with courage and distinction in some of the most difficult and dangerous environments,” he said. “More than 180 brave Pakistani souls gave their lives in the service of peace. We honour their sacrifice.” The chief highlighted Pakistan’s leadership with Denmark on UN Security Council (UNSC) resolution 2823, which strengthened accountability for crimes against UN peacekeepers. One hundred and fifty-three countries co-sponsored the resolution, which according to Guterres, was the largest number of co-sponsors for a UNSC resolution in UN history. The UN chief also shared his plans to visit United Nations Military Observer Group in India and Pakistan (UNMOGIP) later in the day to pay tribute to the mission and to peacekeepers worldwide. Commenting on terrorism in the country, he said: “Pakistan has endured immense suffering. Thousands of people lost their lives. Families and communities across the country continue to bear scars. We stand with Pakistan in confronting this threat of terrorism.” He added that addressing terrorism and legitimate security concerns was necessary and indispensable. “Experience shows that the strongest and most effective security responses are those grounded in international law, human rights and the rule of law.” Towards the end of his speech, Guterres spoke about the climate crisis. “My last visit to Pakistan came during the catastrophic floods of 2022. I will never forget the utter devastation I saw,” he said, referring to the unprecedented floods four years ago that affected approximately 33 million people and claimed the lives of 1,700 people. “But I also saw the resilience, determination and solidarity of the Pakistani people,” Guterres said. “Pakistan is on the frontlines of climate chaos despite contributing only a tiny fraction of global emissions.” He appreciated Pakistan’s response to the crises, including establishment of the Loss and Damage Fund and the country’s growing clean energy transition. However, he asserted that leadership from vulnerable developing countries cannot substitute for responsibility from developed countries. “The G20 represents 80 per cent of global emissions. We need a drastic reduction in those emissions this decade,” he highlighted. “The principle of common but differentiated responsibilities must apply, but all countries must do their part,” he said. Meanwhile, Dar said he “greatly appreciated” Guterres’ visit, which he asserted was a reflection of the “long-standing and close cooperation” between Pakistan and the UN. “It also shows our common resolve to strengthen multilateralism and our cooperation at a time of profound global challenges,” he said. “We have consistently sought to uphold the purposes and principles of the UN charter, advance international peace and security, contribute to peacekeeping and strengthen multilateral solutions to global challenges.” Dar referred to Guterres as a “great friend” of Pakistan, adding that the country would not forget his solidarity during the 2022 floods as well as his efforts to mobilise international support for recovery and reconstruction. During its time as an elected member of the UNSC, Dar said Pakistan had tried to make “significant contributions” to international peace and security, with particular emphasis on dialogue, diplomacy, and the peaceful settlement of disputes. “Our initiative on resolution 2788 on strengthening multilateralism and mechanisms for the peaceful settlement of disputes is a reflection of Pakistan’s approach in this regard,” the minister recalled. “The unanimous adoption of that resolution reaffirmed the importance of negotiation, mediation, preventive diplomacy, and the good offices of the UN secretary general.” He appreciated Guterres’ engagement with the follow-up to the resolution, including the participation and presentation of “solid recommendations” in the open debate held in July this year. Dar said the country valued the secretary general’s “readiness” to extend his good offices in situations where dialogue and diplomacy could help reduce tensions and create space for peaceful solutions. “This is particularly relevant at a time when the international community is confronted with multiple conflicts and crises,” he reiterated. “Pakistan believes that the UN must remain at the centre of international efforts to address these challenges and that diplomacy must be given every opportunity to succeed.” Pakistan, Dar said, had played a “proactive and constructive” role in promoting dialogue and de-escalation in the Gulf region. He appreciated Guterres’ support for Pakistan’s mediation efforts and his recognition of the importance of diplomatic engagement. “Pakistan’s role in facilitating dialogue is consistent with our broader approach at the UN, which is to promote cooperation over confrontation, dialogue over conflict and peaceful settlement over the use of force,” he stated. The minister said Pakistan supported the chief’s UN80 initiative, which seeks to make the UN more “effective, efficient and fit for purpose”. “We believe that efforts to strengthen the organisation must reinforce its ability to deliver on its core mandates, while ensuring that the priorities and concerns of developing countries remain central.” According to him, stronger, effective, inclusive, and representative multilateralism was needed at a time of growing geopolitical tensions, conflicts, humanitarian crises, climate vulnerabilities and economic pressures. He further appreciated the UN chief’s “continued attention” to issues of particular importance to Pakistan, including regional peace and stability, counter-terrorism, climate vulnerability and development challenges. “We also greatly appreciate the UN’s consistent position on the Jammu and Kashmir dispute and the reiteration of the UN framework and UNSC resolutions for resolving the dispute,” he said. Dar said he briefed the UN chief on India’s unilateral move of holding the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) in abeyance , which he referred to as a blatant violation of international law. “We underscored the need to ensure that India stops weaponising water and fulfils its obligations under the IWT.” He also highlighted Pakistan’s “deep concern” at the continued use of Afghan soil for carrying out terrorist attacks against Pakistan. He urged the UN chief and the international community to help address these challenges. Dar meets UN chief Earlier in the day, Dar held a one-on-one meeting with the UN chief, with the two discussing regional and global issues relating to peace and security, the Foreign Office (FO) said. The FO said the discussions covered Palestine, Jammu and Kashmir, Afghanistan, counter-terrorism and the future of multilateralism. Dar briefed the UN secretary general on Pakistan’s positions on Jammu and Kashmir and the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT), reaffirming Islamabad’s call for a just and peaceful resolution of the Kashmir dispute in accordance with relevant UNSC resolutions. According to the FO, Dar also highlighted Pakistan’s diplomatic efforts to promote dialogue and de-escalation, including its facilitation of the Islamabad talks between the US and Iran. He reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to dialogue and diplomacy as the most effective means of resolving disputes. The UN secretary general appreciated Pakistan’s longstanding contribution to the UN, as well as its diplomatic efforts to promote dialogue, mediation and de-escalation, the FO said. President confers Nishan-i-Imtiaz on UN chief President Asif Ali Zardari also conferred the Nishan-i-Imtiaz on Guterres in recognition of his “distinguished international service, leadership of the UN and contribution to global peace and development,” a handout by the President’s Secretariat said. The award, first to any UN secretary general by Pakistan, was conferred in a special investiture ceremony held at Aiwan-i-Sadr, the statement said. According to the handout the president also separately met with the UN chief and appreciated his principled leadership, his efforts for international peace, dialogue, diplomacy and peaceful settlement of disputes, as well as his constructive engagement with Pakistan and attention to the concerns of developing countries. “The president said Pakistan remains steadfast in its support for the Palestinian people and their right to self-determination,” it added. “He appreciated the [UN chief’s] consistent advocacy for Palestinian statehood and a two-state solution and said Pakistan would continue supporting efforts towards implementation of the relevant UNSC resolutions,” the handout detailed. The president further reiterated Pakistan’s commitment to peace and stability in South Asia, stressing that durable peace required sustained dialogue between Pakistan and India and the resolution of all outstanding disputes, particularly Jammu and Kashmir, as agreed under the UN resolutions respecting the sentiments of the Kashmiri people. He also conveyed Pakistan’s position that the IWT was a binding international agreement and could not be unilaterally suspended or placed in abeyance. President Zardari, per the handout, stressed that water should not be used as a weapon and an instrument of political pressure and that Pakistan’s water rights, recognised by international courts, under the treaty must be respected. On the subject of regional peace and diplomacy, Zardari said the country’s diplomatic efforts, including the Islamabad Talks, had been guided by the “imperative of de-escalation, dialogue and protection of human life”. “He reaffirmed Pakistan’s readiness to facilitate diplomacy wherever it could be helpful, stressing that there is no alternative to dialogue for addressing regional disputes,” the handout said. The president also spoke about counter-terrorism and Afghanistan. He said Pakistan remained a “committed partner” in the global fight against terrorism and has made enormous sacrifices in this cause. “Pakistan continues to face terrorism from groups operating from Afghan territory and has shared evidence concerning external support to terrorist proxies targeting Pakistan,” the president said, stressing that Afghan territory must not be used against Pakistan or any other country. UN chief’s visit Guterres arrived in Islamabad in the early hours of Tuesday for a two-day official visit. “Upon arrival, the secretary-general was received by Acting Foreign Secretary Ambassador Nabeel Munir,” the FO said in a post on X. The UN chief also visited the National Disaster Management Authority’s (NDMA) headquarters on the first day of his visit. The visit comes as Guterres’ 10-year tenure as UN chief is set to end on Dec 31. In its Monday statement, the FO said that during Guterres’ visit, Pakistan’s “efforts towards strengthening multilateralism and international peace and security, as well as its strides towards disaster preparedness and early warning, will be highlighted”. PM Shehbaz met Guterres on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York last month. The two discussed major regional and international developments, including the situation in the Middle East. In that meeting, Guterres commended Pakistan’s role and strong voice at the UN, as well as its contribution to international peace and security. The UN chief also appreciated Pakistan’s role and sacrifices in countering terrorism. Guterres’ first visit to Pakistan as the UN secretary general was in February 2020, about three years after he was elected to the position in 2016.

items.title: Olympic qualifiers: Oshoala, Plumptre absent as 21 players hit Super Falcons camp
items.description: By Adegboyega Adeleye Twenty-one Super Falcons players have arrived in camp in Ikenne, Ogun State, as preparations intensify for Nigeria’s 2028 Olympic qualifying double-header against Comoros, with star forwards Asisat Oshoala and defender Ashleigh Plumptre among the notable absentees. The Falcons shared the latest camp update on their official handle on Tuesday evening, captioning the post, “Camp update: 21 players in.” Camp update: 21 players in … pic.twitter.com/y5skvKdNXt — NGSuper_Falcons (@NGSuper_Falcons) October 6, 2026 Oshoala and Plumptre were both included in the original squad invited by interim head coach Augustine Eguavoen but will not feature in the upcoming fixtures. According to the Nigeria Football Federation (NFF), Plumptre, who had been recalled after missing the 2026 Women’s Africa Cup of Nations through injury, asked to be excused because of a ligament injury while six-time African Player of the Year, Oshoala, also pleaded to be excused. Eguavoen subsequently called up Belarus-based former U-20 forward Blessing Okpe as a replacement for Oshoala. Also unavailable, according to the NFF, are Benfica defender Oluwatosin Demehin and forward Flourish Sabastine, who are said to be dealing with residency permit requirements in Portugal, further reducing the squad interim coach Austin Eguavoen initially selected for the qualifiers. Eguavoen has also released Oluwakemi Adegbuyi and Favour Nkwocha to join Nigeria’s under-17 women’s team ahead of the FIFA Under-17 Women’s World Cup in Morocco. Adegbuyi was named the most valuable player at the recent WAFU-B Under-17 Girls Cup, while Nkwocha was part of Nigeria’s squad at the Under-20 Women’s World Cup in Poland. The withdrawals leave Eguavoen needing to reshape his squad just days before Friday’s first leg at the Remo Stars Stadium in Ikenne, where both matches of the second-round tie will be played. The latest 21-player camp list comprises Christiana Uzoma, Farida Abdulwahab, Tumininu Adeshina, Valentina Uroko, Glory Edet, Shukurat Oladipo, Glory Ogbonna, Suliat Abideen, Favour Omenazu, Joy Igbokwe, Fatimoh Solaty, Toni Payne, Christy Ucheibe, Shakirat Moshood, Blessing Nkor, Folashade Ijamilusi, Janet Akekoromowei, Rasheedat Ajibade, Jennifer Echegini and Michelle Alozie. Players currently in camp Christiana Uzoma Farida Abdulwahab Tumininu Adeshina Valentina Uroko Glory Edet Shukurat Oladipo Glory Ogbonna Suliat Abideen Sandra John Favour Omenazu Joy Igbokwe Fatimoh Solaty Toni Payne Christy Ucheibe Jennifer Echegini Shakirat Moshood Blessing Nkor Folashade Ijamilusi Janet Akekoromowei Rasheedat Ajibade Michelle Alozie The current camp composition reflects a mixture of established internationals and new faces, including Favour Omenazu, the MK Dons captain who has received her maiden Super Falcons call-up. Nigeria received a bye into the second round of the Olympic qualifying series as one of the three highest-ranked teams in the competition, while Comoros advanced after a remarkable 30-0 aggregate victory over Sudan. Both legs of the second-round tie will be played at the Remo Stars Stadium, Ikenne-Remo, because Comoros does not have a CAF-approved venue. The first leg is scheduled for Friday, October 9, with the return leg billed for Tuesday, October 13. The Falcons are seeking a return to the Olympic Games after making their comeback at Paris 2024, following a 16-year absence from the competition. Nigeria had secured that ticket by edging South Africa 1-0 on aggregate in the final qualifying round. The road to Los Angeles, however, remains long, with Africa allocated only two places in the 2028 women’s football tournament. Nigeria must negotiate four knockout rounds to secure one of them. A victory over Comoros on aggregate would send the Falcons into the third round, where either Morocco or the Democratic Republic of Congo awaits. The Olympic campaign also comes at a crucial point for the Falcons following their disappointing 2026 WAFCON campaign, which ended with a quarter-final defeat to Cameroon and cost Nigeria an automatic route to the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup. Eguavoen, appointed interim coach in September, is therefore tasked with steering the team through the Olympic qualifying campaign as Nigeria seeks to return to the Games in Los Angeles. Vanguard News The post Olympic qualifiers: Oshoala, Plumptre absent as 21 players hit Super Falcons camp appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Campagne agricole : Le commandant Ismaël Sombié visite un bas-fond rizicole à Komki-Ipala et une ferme à Saaba
items.description: Dans le cadre du suivi de la campagne agricole 2026-2027 dans le Kadiogo, le commandant Ismaël Sombié, ministre d'État, chargé de l'Agriculture, a effectué, ce 6 octobre 2026, une visite terrain dans une ferme à Saaba et un bas-fond rizicole à Komki-Ipala . Le ministre a commencé sa visite dans la ferme d'un entrepreneur agricole de 7 hectares. Elle a été créée en 2021 avec pour objectif la production laitière. La ferme comprend 151 têtes de vaches métissés dont 81 holstein, 55 Montbéliard et 15 têtes de Goudali. Elle produit également du poisson dont 30 tonnes de tilapias et 60 tonnes de clarias. En plus de la production de la volaille, il y a la production fourragère, notamment le maralfalfa et le Azzola. Après la ferme, le commandant Ismaël Sombié s'est rendu sur l'exploitation rizicole de Tintilou dans la commune de Komki-Ipala. La superficie totale exploitée est de 30 hectares. Ce sont 312 exploitants, dont 182 femmes qui y cultivent du riz de type Orylux. Au passage du ministre, les cultures étaient au stade de maturation. Selon les techniciens, la physionomie présage une bonne récolte. Une vache laitière de la ferme©️Faso7 « Ça permet de dire que en tout cas, au niveau de la campagne hivernale au niveau du Kadiogo, les perspectives seront bonnes si vraiment on arrive à avoir les pluies jusqu'à la première décade du mois d'octobre » , a expliqué Aïcha Sana, directrice régionale en charge de l'agriculture du Kadiogo. Elle a ajouté que dans la région du Kadiogo, les pluies se sont installées tardivement avec une répartition irrégulière. En dépit de cela, la situation s'est stabilisée avec l'avènement de la pluie à une certaine période. Elle a souligné que pour le Kadiogo, il est attendu 65 000 tonnes de céréales. « On va espérer qu'il pleuve jusqu'à au 10 octobre pour vraiment permettre aux cultures d'être à maturation pour qu'on atteigne vraiment les objectifs », a-t-elle souhaité. L'exploitation agricole de Kpmki-Ipala©️Faso7 Les femmes de la coopérative ont saisi l'occasion de la visite du ministre pour lui exprimer leur reconnaissance. Elles ont rappelé que son département les a accompagnées en leur offrant des semences, des engrais de qualité et des étuveuses. Toutefois, elles ont exprimé le souhait d'avoir un forage afin de pratiquer la culture maraîchère après la récolte du riz. Séance tenante, leur souhait a trouvé une oreille attentive. En effet, au regard de la volonté affichée de ces femmes, le ministre a indiqué qu'il mettra un forage à leur disposition incessamment afin qu'elles puissent produire pendant la saison sèche. Cheick Habib Désiré BAYILI Faso7 L’article Campagne agricole : Le commandant Ismaël Sombié visite un bas-fond rizicole à Komki-Ipala et une ferme à Saaba est apparu en premier sur Faso7 .

items.title: Almost 500 arrested, over 40 police wounded in French school protests
items.description: At least 488 people were arrested and 43 members of the security forces wounded Tuesday as tens of thousands massed in France to protest against poor conditions in schools, the interior ministry said. Most of the day’s demonstrations were peaceful but there were sporadic clashes across the country with protesters throwing projectiles and security forces using tear gas, AFP correspondents said. Late evening, protesters were locked in an uneasy standoff with members of the security forces in Place de la Nation in eastern Paris as the main demonstration in the French capital wound down without dispersing. Since last week, at least 6,547 people have been arrested over the protests, the interior ministry added. The ministry said earlier some 256,000 people had protested nationwide on Tuesday. items.title: N2.7 trillion allegation against monarch is untrue – Olu of Warri ‘s aide
items.description: By Jimitota Onoyume The Sole Representative of the Olu of Warri, Ogiame Atuwatse III, to the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPCL) and its Joint Venture partners, Prince Collins Edema, has dismissed as untrue claims that the monarch receives N2.7 trillion annually from a pipeline surveillance contract. Reacting to an allegation by His Majesty Asari Dokubo-Asari, Amanyanabo of the Source, Elem Kalabari (Torusarama Piri), Rivers state, in a trending video on social media, in which he claimed the Olu of Warri earns such a sum annually from the pipeline surveillance job Edema in a statement yesterday said the allegation was devoid of facts. The statement reads: “The attention of the Sole Representative of His Majesty Ogiame Atuwatse III, CFR, the Olu of Warri to NNPC Limited, has been drawn to the recent public allegation by Mr. Asari Dokubo that His Majesty receives the sum of N2.7 trillion annually from pipeline surveillance contracts. “Given the extraordinary nature of this allegation, its potential implications for the reputation of the Olu of Warri, and, more importantly, the strategic importance of pipeline surveillance to the Nigerian state, we consider it necessary to respond publicly and directly to the relevant institutions of the Federal Government. “For the avoidance of doubt, the allegation that the Olu of Warri receives N2.7 trillion annually from pipeline surveillance contracts is categorically rejected. “We challenge Mr. Dokubo to produce the documentary evidence upon which this extraordinary claim is based. “If there are concerns about a pipeline-security arrangement, the relevant contracts, procurement processes, corporate records, government approvals, performance reports and regulatory documents should be examined. If wrongdoing is alleged, the appropriate institutions should investigate and establish the facts. And if no wrongdoing is established, politically charged allegations should not be allowed to substitute for evidence.” The post N2.7 trillion allegation against monarch is untrue – Olu of Warri ‘s aide appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: 4 FBR officials, traffic policeman martyred in DI Khan attacks: police
items.description: DERA ISMAIL KHAN: Four Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) officials were martyred in firing by unidentified assailants near Qureshi Mor in Dera Ismail Khan, while a separate attack on a highway traffic police mobile near the Mufti Mahmood Chowk bypass left a constable martyred and another injured, police said on Tuesday. Dera Ismail Khan District Police Officer Ziauddin Ahmad told Dawn that two of the four FBR officials were serving with the board on a contractual basis. The assailants fled after the attacks, prompting police to cordon off the areas and launch search operations, the police added. An investigation into the incidents is underway. In the other attack near the Mufti Mahmood Chowk bypass, unidentified assailants opened fire on a highway traffic police mobile, martyring the police official driving the vehicle. Another official was injured and taken to the District Headquarters Teaching Hospital for treatment, police said. Senior police officials visited the hospital following the attacks and reviewed the situation, according to the police. Later, a police statement said the martyred traffic police constable and two of the FBR officials had been laid to rest. The funeral prayers for Highway Traffic Police Constable Habib and and FBR officials Rehmatullah and Sulaiman were held at Ejaz Shaheed Police Lines, the statement said. Police personnel presented a guard of honor to the deceased, while officials laid floral wreaths on the bodies and prayed for the departed souls, it added. The funeral prayers were attended by MNA Faisal Amin Gandapur, DI Khan Commissioner Dawar Khan, Station Commander Brigadier Salman Adil Shah, Regional Police Officer (RPO) Ghulam Mubashir Maken, DPO Ziauddin Ahmed, FBR officials, senior police and security officers, representatives of other government departments, political and social figures and relatives of the deceased. Speaking on the occasion, RPO Ghulam Mubashir Maken said the sacrifices of the martyrs would not go in vain, and the fight against terrorism would continue with full resolve. He said the sacrifices of the personnel were a source of pride for the state and the nation and assured the bereaved families that the state would not leave them alone and would provide them with all possible support. “Such cowardly attacks can not weaken our resolve,” the RPO said, adding that police and other law enforcement agencies were united and committed to eliminating terrorism. He described the martyred personnel as national heroes and said their sacrifices would further strengthen the resolve of law enforcement agencies to continue their efforts for peace and security. President Asif Ali Zardari also expressed grief over the martyrdom of the officials and the constable and concern over terrorism incidents in the district, according to a statement posted on X. He . “The president stated that the people of Pakistan and security agencies stand like an iron wall against terrorism fuelled by foreign patronage and local facilitators. He affirmed that the Pakistani people would carry this struggle to its logical conclusion,” the statement said. He expressed his condolences to the bereaved families and prayed for the recovery of the injured. Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb also strongly condemned the firing incident at Qureshi Mor, a statement by his ministry said. “He paid tribute to Arm Guard Rahmatullah and Sepoy Sulaiman, who lost their lives in the line of duty. He also extended his profound condolences to the bereaved families and prayed for the departed souls to rest in eternal peace,” the statement read. It further quoted the minister as saying that the “tragic incident is a matter of deep grief for the entire FBR fraternity. Our thoughts and prayers are with the families of the martyred officials.” Aurangzeb directed that all relevant aspects of the incident be pursued in coordination with the concerned authorities and expressed the hope that the perpetrators would be identified and brought to justice, the statement said. Meanwhile, mobile phone services, which had remained suspended across DI Khan district for three days, were restored, providing relief to residents and traders. The prolonged suspension had disrupted communication and affected routine commercial and public activities across the district. The restoration of mobile services also came after the postponement of the second annual matriculation examinations scheduled to begin on Oct 7. Controller of Examinations Qaiser Anwar had announced that the examinations scheduled from Oct 7 to 10 would be rescheduled, with the new examination schedule beginning on Oct 12. The authorities have not publicly linked the suspension of mobile phone services to the attacks. Further details about the circumstances surrounding the incidents and the identity of the assailants were not immediately available. KP has been witnessing terrorist attacks and security challenges for a long time. Sept 2026 particularly witnessed a significant deterioration in Pakistan’s overall security environment, accompanied by growing political, economic and regional pressures, according to Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS) . Militant violence increased substantially , with 225 attacks recorded nationwide, compared with 199 in August, representing a 13.1 per cent increase and the highest monthly total recorded in 12 years. On Sept 27 , 14 people, including two rescue officials, were martyred and 35 sustained injuries after a suicide bomber rammed an explosive-laden vehicle into a police checkpost in and then targeted an ambulance taking bodies to hospital in DI Khan. On Sept 18, a major attack in the old Police Lines in KP’s Kohat claimed 23 lives and injured about 100 others. Eight terrorists were killed during an overnight clearance operation .

items.title: Mali: les forces armées reprennent Kidal
items.description: Les Forces armées maliennes (FAMa) ont repris le contrôle de Kidal, une ville située à environ 1 530 kilomètres au Nord de Bamako, ce mardi 6 octobre 2026, selon plusieurs sources médiatiques. L’armée malienne est entrée de nouveau à Kidal, la capitale de la région du Nord du pays qui était assiégée par les groupes rebelles et autres terroristes depuis quelques mois. Plusieurs sources médiatiques confirment cette information après avoir contacté des officiers de l’armée malienne qui ont mené plusieurs heures d'opérations avec l’appui de leurs partenaires russes, dans la région de Kidal. Dans un communiqué publié avant l’entrée des forces maliennes dans la ville, l’état-major général des armées avait indiqué que les FAMa et leurs partenaires russes avaient engagé des «opérations aéroterrestres d’envergure» dans le cadre de la réadaptation du dispositif de l’opération «Dougoukoloko». Le communiqué précise que ces opérations visent notamment à «traquer et neutraliser les groupes armés terroristes» opérant dans la région, détruire leurs «sanctuaires et leurs réseaux d’approvisionnement» et restaurer la sécurité des populations ainsi que la libre circulation des personnes et des biens. L’état-major avait également appelé les populations de la région au «calme et à la vigilance», tout en les exhortant à poursuivre leur coopération avec les forces de défense et de sécurité. Par Wakat Séra L’article Mali: les forces armées reprennent Kidal est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Le directeur de l’AFD constate les réalisations du PAREC au CEG Avéta
items.description: Lomé, 6 oct. (ATOP) – Le directeur de l’Agence française de développement (AFD), Benjamin Neumann, a visité, le mardi 6 octobre à Avéta, dans la commune Zio 1, les infrastructures du CEG Avéta, réalisées dans le cadre du Programme d’appui à la réforme des collèges (PAREC), arrivé à son terme au Togo. L’un des bâtiments scolaires Le projet a permis à l’établissement de disposer de nouvelles infrastructures destinées à améliorer les conditions d’apprentissage et de travail. Le CEG Avéta a notamment bénéficié de deux blocs pédagogiques de quatre salles de classe chacun, d’un bloc administratif comprenant un bureau, un secrétariat, une salle des professeurs et un bureau partagé entre le Conseiller principal d’éducation (CPE) et le directeur adjoint. Quatre blocs sanitaires ont également été construits. L’établissement a par ailleurs reçu des bancs, des manuels et des kits scolaires ainsi que des guides destinés aux chefs d’établissement. Après une première phase mise en œuvre de 2014 à 2018, le PAREC II, déployé de 2020 à 2025, a accompagné 176 collèges publics dans les cinq régions éducatives du Togo. Le programme a permis la construction de 384 salles de classe équipées, ainsi que des blocs administratifs, des latrines, des forages et des installations solaires. Ces réalisations ont bénéficié à plus de 45 000 élèves. La Directrice témoignant sa gratitude à l’AFD Financé sous forme de dons par l’AFD et mis en œuvre avec les autorités togolaises, le PAREC accompagne la réforme de l’enseignement au collège en intervenant notamment sur les infrastructures, la qualité des apprentissages et les conditions de scolarisation. Le programme accorde une attention particulière à l’équité entre les filles et les garçons et au renforcement des capacités d’accueil des établissements, notamment en milieu rural. Le directeur de l’AFD a réaffirmé l’engagement de la France à accompagner le Togo dans le secteur de l’éducation et en faveur de la réussite des jeunes. Il a souligné que les infrastructures réalisées contribuent à améliorer les conditions de travail des enseignants et d’apprentissage des élèves. La directrice du CEG Avéta, Dongo Ablavi Bileyo, a estimé que ces nouveaux bâtiments contribueront à améliorer durablement les performances scolaires de l’établissement et les conditions d’épanouissement des élèves. A travers ses interventions dans de nombreux pays, l’AFD accompagne des projets liés notamment à l’éducation et au développement durable, en partenariat avec les autorités et les acteurs locaux. ATOP/AR/AO

items.title: Kintinian : une rentrée scolaire 2026-2027 à deux vitesses, entre forte mobilisation et défaillances locales
items.description: La rentrée scolaire 2026-2027 s’est ouverte sous le signe du contraste dans la nouvelle préfecture de Bouré Kintinian. Si la rentrée administrative du 21 septembre laissait présager une préparation rigoureuse, la réalité du terrain offre un spectacle à deux vitesses. Notre constat mené à Boukaria et à Kintinian-centre montre que l’élan massif des élèves et des enseignants se heurte, par endroits, à une défaillance flagrante des autorités locales et des structures d’encadrement. Dans la majeure partie de la localité, le civisme et le droit ont primé. De Boukaria jusqu’au centre-ville de Kintinian, les feux étaient au vert. Les enseignants ont répondu présents et les élèves ont massivement investi les salles de classe dès les premières heures. Cette ferveur s’est particulièrement illustrée au Lycée-Collège du centre-ville de Kintinian, où l’ambiance était totale. Face à des salles combles et à un corps professoral mobilisé, le proviseur s’est dit pleinement satisfait de cette reprise effective. Une preuve que, là où l’encadrement joue son rôle, la rentrée est une réussite. Le tableau s’assombrit radicalement dès que l’on s’éloigne du centre-ville. À Bouré Setiguia et à Bouré Balato, le démarrage a été plombé par des manquements inacceptables. Si le personnel d’encadrement a tenté de sauver les meubles en se présentant dans les écoles, l’absence presque totale des élèves trahit un manque cruel de sensibilisation et de suivi de la part des leaders communautaires. Le summum du paradoxe et du laisser-aller se situe à l’école primaire publique de Bouré Balato. Dans cet établissement, le constat est tout simplement accablant : classes vides, enseignants absents. Sur les lieux, seul le nouveau directeur, livré à lui-même, errait dans un décor de désolation. Ce dernier, qui venait à peine d’arriver officiellement, n’a pas caché son amertume face à notre micro : «Moi je viens de prendre service seulement hièr. J'ai trouvé que rien n'est fait: la cour est impropre, les salles de classes vides,les bancs cassés, et beaucoup d'autres anomalies» a-t- déploré avec impuissance. Cette situation met directement en lumière la démission totale des présidents de districts et des bureaux de l’APEAE de Balato et de Setiguia. En abandonnant les écoles à leur triste sort, sans aucun travail préalable d’assainissement, de préparation du mobilier ou de mobilisation des parents, ces acteurs indispensables ont failli à leur mission élémentaire. En conclusion, si la rentrée 2026-2027 est réussie au centre-ville de Kintinian, elle reste profondément entachée par l’inertie constatée à la périphérie. Le délaissement des infrastructures par les présidents de districts et la passivité des bureaux de l’APEAE de Setiguia et de Balato constituent un sérieux point noir. Pour que la nouvelle préfecture de Bouré Kintinian brille par son système éducatif, les autorités préfectorales doivent impérativement sanctionner ce relâchement et contraindre les responsables locaux à assumer pleinement leurs responsabilités envers la jeunesse. Mamoudou Kéïta, correspondant à Kintinian. 628 61 88 90 L’article Kintinian : une rentrée scolaire 2026-2027 à deux vitesses, entre forte mobilisation et défaillances locales est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Mandate of the UN Special Rapporteur on Russia Extended for Another Year
items.description: The UN Human Rights Council on October 6 extended the mandate of the Special Rapporteur on the human rights situation in Russia for another year. Russia withdrew its amendment that attempted to delete renewal of the mandate. Click to expand Image The "Broken Chair” in front of the Palais Nations, Geneva, September 22, 2026. © 2026 Tanya Lokshina/Human Rights Watch The extension is welcome news. The Russia mandate provides an essential independent voice to document the Russian government’s grave human rights violations and serves as a lifeline for the country’s besieged civil society. The mandate was established in 2022 when, along with its war against Ukraine, the Kremlin launched a draconian crackdown on human rights defenders, independent journalists, political opponents, and other Russian based critics of the war. With the Ukraine war now in its fifth year, the Kremlin continues to escalate the crackdown on virtually all forms of dissent. There are over 1,800 political prisoners in Russia. The authorities have branded more individuals and organizations “undesirable” or “foreign agents”—labels used to stigmatize critics as enemies of the state—and targeted leading international human rights groups. They have also expanded the use of “extremist” designations against Russian human rights organizations, as well as LGBT people and their supporters. The crackdown has also intensified on digital freedoms, as authorities seek to isolate Russians from information critical of the government and to restrict access to online services and information they perceive as “hostile.” As UN Special Rapporteur Mariana Katzarova highlighted in her latest report, the Kremlin has increasingly resorted to transnational repression against exiled critics. Russia adopted in August legislation imposing restrictions on Russians abroad who have been convicted of offenses that are predominantly used in politically motivated prosecutions. The restrictions include denying consular services, such as passport renewals and notarial services; blocking access to government digital services; and freezing bank accounts and other assets in Russia. With human rights defenders, journalists, and activists imprisoned, forced into exile, or otherwise silenced, the Special Rapporteur’s mandate is more important than ever. Its renewal recognizes that intensifying repression inside Russia—and efforts to extend it beyond Russia’s borders—requires sustained international scrutiny. The Council should ensure that the Special Rapporteur has the support necessary to document these abuses, engage with Russian civil society, and ensure that repression is not rendered invisible.

items.title: Trump’s Unlikely Strategy to Control History: Footnotes
items.description: Most of Donald Trump’s efforts to control the nation’s largest museum complex have been loud. He tried to fire a Smithsonian museum director on social media, ordered the placement of warning signs outside its American-history museum, and demanded that the museum take down a modernist sculpture he dislikes. But while this political theater plays out publicly, the White House’s Office of Management and Budget is quietly using an obscure funding power as part of its campaign to influence how the Smithsonian tells the American story. Late last month, according to previously unreported public records, OMB included a footnote in two recent apportionments of federal funds that conditions nearly $190 million for the Smithsonian on the institution’s compliance with Trump’s March 2025 executive order accusing it of spreading “divisive narratives.” Essentially, the White House is trying to force adherence to its preferred version of history through a little-known but legally binding budget mechanism. The fiscal-year-2027 footnote, which applies to funds carried over from last year in two of the Smithsonian’s main salaries and expenses accounts, reads: To the extent permitted by law, amounts apportioned shall be available for obligation in a manner consistent with Executive Order 14253 (March 27, 2025), “Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History.” That executive order marked the beginning of the Trump administration’s campaign to change the Smithsonian, alleging that the institution had come “under the influence of a divisive, race-centered ideology” and prohibiting “expenditure on exhibits or programs that degrade shared American values, divide Americans based on race, or promote programs or ideologies inconsistent with Federal law and policy.” The footnote does not specify how the Smithsonian should apply the order’s vague prohibition. But it is more than simply a threat: Apportionment footnotes are enforceable under the Antideficiency Act, the violation of which can carry criminal penalties . Such footnotes are one of several tactics that the Trump administration has used to try to supplant Congress’s spending power. In this case, the footnote suggests that the fight over the Smithsonian’s purpose goes much deeper than Trump’s most visible attacks. Today, the Smithsonian is nearly two-thirds federally funded and receives an annual total appropriation of about $1 billion—a reality that would have agonized some of its earliest supporters. In a way, John Quincy Adams could be said to have foreseen what Trump is trying to do to the Smithsonian: In 1842, the former president, then serving in Congress, opposed a bill providing federal funds to the Smithsonian, writing that the new institution in Washington, D.C., should be “exclusively confined to itself and not entangled or commingled with any national establishment requiring appropriations of public money.” Even Joseph Henry, the first Smithsonian secretary, under whom the institution began receiving regular federal funding to support a museum, worried about it, writing in an 1877 letter that the museum was “liable to be brought under direct political influence.” If there is any constant in American life, Adams and Henry knew it then and Trump knows it now: Money is control. Although the Trump administration has notched only small wins against the Smithsonian, it’s been playing money games since last year with an institution that is meant to operate independently. Starting in September of last year , OMB began adding footnotes demanding that the Smithsonian comply with two documents: the March executive order and an August letter to Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch insisting that exhibition materials and other documents be turned over for a content review. Then, starting in April of this year , the footnote was revised to require the Smithsonian to follow Trump’s budget request rather than the 2026 appropriations bill Congress had passed—essentially telling the Smithsonian to operate at a $89 million deficit from what lawmakers had legislated. After several iterations, that footnote was ultimately removed on July 2. Two days later, the White House issued a scathing report on the National Museum of American History. At that point, the footnotes tactic seemed to have gone dormant. Until late last month. It is unclear whether the footnotes have had any concrete impacts on the Smithsonian’s operations. The Smithsonian declined a request for an interview about the footnotes and the White House did not answer questions about the matter. Representative Chellie Pingree, a Maine Democrat who is the ranking member on the House appropriations subcommittee that oversees the Smithsonian, told me she spoke with Bunch this summer about the funding issues and got the sense that the institution was waiting to push back until the footnotes really interfered with its work. The footnotes were never challenged, she said. “I think they caused enormous heartburn for the Smithsonian. Eventually, the funds were released, and so now my worry has turned to what will happen on the next round.” Senator Jeff Merkley, an Oregon Democrat who is also the minority leader on a subcommittee tasked with Smithsonian oversight, condemned what he described as the refusal to release tens of millions of dollars earlier this year. “OMB used small footnotes to make a huge, absurd assertion that holding funding to the President’s budget level—just a number on a piece of paper—overrode the actual law,” he wrote to me. “In fact, it is illegal to withhold such funding.” Multiple budget experts told me these footnotes are very strange. Cerin Lindgrensavage, a lawyer at the nonpartisan watchdog group Protect Democracy, has been following apportionments closely and told me that the Smithsonian footnotes were so bespoke that a tracker that her organization had made did not flag them. “It never occurred to us that somebody would put something so egregious in text,” she said. In particular, “the idea that you would resurrect the president’s request that has zero force of law from an earlier part of the appropriations process and impose it at the very end is abhorrent to the rule of law and the constitutional order as we know it,” she said. [ Read: The next change Trump has planned for the Smithsonian ] This context makes Trump’s 2027 budget request even more ominous for the Smithsonian, because it’s the lowest for the institution in years. At $961.3 million, Trump’s proposal cuts spending by about 11 percent from the previous year. The request also stresses the importance of maintaining and protecting museums on the National Mall, which is home to about half of the Smithsonian’s museums and ground zero for Trump’s pet projects in Washington. The White House has used footnotes against other federal entities, including the National Science Foundation . Last month, a judge ruled against the Trump administration in a case about Education Department apportionments, writing that the government’s use of restrictive footnotes to force compliance with executive orders in this situation was unlawful. Remaining claims in the case, including those related to OMB using apportionments to withhold money from specific programs the administration doesn’t like, are pending. (Lindgrensavage is one of the plaintiffs’ lawyers.) Little attention has been paid to these behind-the-scenes tensions at the Smithsonian, except for when The Washington Sun reported on some of the footnotes earlier this year. The White House has justified its broader campaign by claiming that the Smithsonian presents an overly negative version of U.S. history and that its leadership has a political agenda. Historians have decried the Trump administration’s attempt to influence the institution, and Democratic lawmakers have introduced legislation to protect the Smithsonian’s independence. Smithsonian leadership has occasionally pushed back against the administration’s wider claims, saying its work is nonpartisan and rooted in scholarship. But the face-off coincides with an ongoing debate over how to tell American history. Should it be one overarching narrative or comprise many smaller, varied perspectives? Should it focus on national unity or diversity? These questions are especially top of mind at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, which is widely seen as measured in its work and has followed larger curatorial and academic trends of widening the historical narrative to include more groups while emphasizing the complexities of the American story. Whatever the approach, history at the Smithsonian has been the responsibility of curators, not presidents. But the Smithsonian is in a particularly vulnerable period. Bunch will retire from his post at the end of the year. Citizen members keep dropping off the Smithsonian’s Board of Regents when their terms expire, and their seats are going unfilled, reportedly because the White House is trying to influence the new picks, The New York Time s wrote this summer. Museum-director positions are open across the institution too—last week, the director of the National Museum of Natural History announced that he is stepping down—adding to a number of major vacancies. For a president seeking control, a power vacuum and a fraying institution could represent an opportunity. One staffer who requested anonymity because she was not authorized to speak on the record told me after Bunch’s retirement announcement that some employees worried that the president might attempt to appoint a secretary, just as he “fired” National Portrait Gallery Director Kim Sajet in a Truth Social post last year. (The Smithsonian said Trump did not have the authority to do that, but she ultimately stepped down anyway). “I think you’d have to really stick your head in the sand to not feel some level of anxiety around this,” the staffer said. In a sense, the White House’s efforts have already worked simply by placing an entire museum system on edge. It has a lot to lose. At the Smithsonian, private money goes toward the glossier endeavors, such as groundbreaking exhibitions and new facilities, while public money is typically used for basic needs, such as operations, conservation of national collections, and maintenance. Public funding keeps the doors open, which is why the institution’s unusual status as a private-public entity is most visible when it has to close during a government shutdown, as happened last year. The footnote tactic exploits that vulnerability. Although the apportionment process was designed to help prevent entities receiving federal dollars from overspending, it is “not an invitation to the Office of Management and Budget to micromanage the federal government,” Lindgrensavage said. The Trump administration has tested the limits of its apportionment authority. More recently, the president has called for a sweeping cancellation of about $810 million in federal dollars, much of it coming out of resources for “refugees, asylees, and other non-citizens,” according to a White House memo . Senator Susan Collins, a Maine Republican, posted on X that OMB was trying “to undermine Congress’s Constitutional power of the purse.” Budgeting experts stressed to me that every line of a footnote is intentional and has a story behind it. In the Smithsonian’s case, the footnotes go into very specific detail. In the version of the footnote that OMB added this spring, the office proposed imposing travel restrictions on the Smithsonian, with exceptions for two projects that Trump is fond of: the semiquincentennial festivities and the Arabian leopards at the National Zoo (which are supported by a gift from Saudi Arabia). In 1839, Adams wrote that he feared a Smithsonian bequest might be “squandered upon cormorants,” referring to voracious birds. Adams was prescient in his anxieties about the Smithsonian’s financial entanglements; he just had the wrong animal. Instead, the Smithsonian’s main antagonist is a devotee of big cats.
